paragraphs: He led the way with these words, and the others followed with a shout that tore the air. Then Zeus, lord of thunder, sent a blast of mighty wind down from the mountains of Ida, and it carried the dust toward the ships. In this way he lulled the Achaeans into feeling secure, and he gave victory to Hector and the Trojans. They trusted in their own strength and in the signs he had shown them, and they tried to break through the great wall of the Achaeans. They tore the breastworks off the walls and threw down the battlements. They heaved up the buttresses, which the Achaeans had planted in front of the wall to hold it up. Once these were pulled down, the Trojans felt sure they would break through the wall. But the Danaans showed no sign of giving ground. They kept the battlements fenced with their shields of ox-hide, and hurled missiles down on any enemy who came below the wall.

The two Ajaxes went all along the walls, cheering on the Achaeans. They spoke kindly to some, and sharply to anyone they saw holding back. “My friends,” they cried, “Argives one and all—good, bad and indifferent, for there was never yet a fight in which all were equal in prowess—there is work enough now for all of you, as you very well know. Make sure that none of you turns in flight toward the ships, daunted by the shouting of the enemy. Press forward and keep one another’s courage up. Perhaps Olympian Zeus, lord of lightning, will grant that we repel our foes and drive them back toward the city.”

So the two went about shouting and urging the Achaeans on. The stones fell as thickly as the flakes of snow on a winter’s day, when Zeus is minded to snow and show mankind these arrows of his. He lulls the wind to rest and snows hour after hour, until he has buried the tops of the high mountains, the headlands that jut into the sea, the grassy plains and the tilled fields of men. The snow lies deep on the forelands and the harbors of the gray sea, but the waves rolling in hold it back so that it can come no further, though everything else is wrapped as in a mantle, so heavy are the heavens with snow. Just so thickly did the stones fall on both sides, some thrown at the Trojans, and some by the Trojans at the Achaeans, and the whole wall was in an uproar.

The Trojans and brave Hector would still not have broken down the gates and the great bar, if Zeus had not turned his son Sarpedon against the Argives, like a lion against a herd of horned cattle. Sarpedon held before him his shield of hammered bronze, which the smith had beaten so fair and round and lined with ox-hides, fastening them with rivets of gold all around the shield. He held this in front of him and brandished two spears, and he came on like a lion of the wilderness that has long been famished for want of meat and will dare to break even into a well-fenced homestead to get at the sheep. The lion may find shepherds keeping watch over their flocks with dogs and spears, but he has no mind to be driven from the fold before he has made his try. Either he will spring on a sheep and carry it off, or a strong hand will hit him with a spear. In just that way Sarpedon was eager to attack the wall and break down its battlements. Then he said to Glaucus son of Hippolochus, “Glaucus, why do we in Lycia receive special honor in our place at table? Why are the choicest portions served to us and our cups kept brimming, and why do men look up to us as though we were gods? Besides, we hold a large estate by the banks of the river Xanthus, fair with orchard lawns and wheat-growing land. So it is right for us to take our stand at the head of all the Lycians and bear the brunt of the fight. Then one man can say to another, ‘Our princes in Lycia eat the fat of the land and drink the best wine, but they are fine fellows. They fight well and are always at the front in battle.’ My good friend, if we could get out of this fight and then escape old age and death forever after, I would neither press forward myself nor tell you to. But death in ten thousand shapes hangs always over our heads, and no man can elude him. So let us go forward and either win glory for ourselves or yield it to another.”

Glaucus listened to what he said, and the pair at once led on the host of Lycians. Menestheus son of Peteos was dismayed when he saw them, for they were coming against his part of the wall, bringing destruction with them. He looked along the wall for some chieftain to support his comrades, and he saw the two Ajaxes, men always eager for the fray, with Teucer, who had just come from his tent, standing near them. But he could not make his voice heard by shouting to them, so great was the uproar of crashing shields and helmets and the battering at the gates, a din that reached the skies. All the gates had been closed, and the Trojans were hammering at them to try to break through. So Menestheus sent Thootes with a message to Ajax. “Run, good Thootes,” he said, “and call Ajax—or better still, tell both to come, for it will soon be all over with us here. The leaders of the Lycians are upon us, men who have always fought desperately before. But if they have too much on their hands to come, then at least let Ajax son of Telamon come, and let Teucer, the famous bowman, come with him.”

The messenger did as he was told. He ran along the wall of the Achaeans until he reached the Ajaxes, and said to them, “Sirs, princes of the Argives, the son of noble Peteos begs you to go to him for a while and help. It would be best if you both came, or it will soon be all over with him. The leaders of the Lycians are upon him, men who have always fought desperately in the past. If you are too busy for both to leave, then Ajax son of Telamon must come at least, and Teucer, the famous bowman, with him.”

Great Ajax son of Telamon heard the message and spoke at once to the son of Oileus. “Ajax,” he said, “you two, yourself and brave Lycomedes, must stay here and keep the Danaans fighting as hard as they can. I am going over there to take my part in the fray. As soon as I have given them the help they need, I will come straight back.”

Ajax son of Telamon set off at once, and Teucer, his brother by the same father, went too, with Pandion carrying Teucer’s bow. They went along inside the wall. They came to the tower where Menestheus was, and found him hard pressed indeed. The brave captains and leaders of the Lycians were storming the battlements like a thick dark cloud, fighting at close quarters and raising the battle cry aloud.

First, Ajax son of Telamon killed brave Epicles, a comrade of Sarpedon. He hit him with a jagged stone that lay by the battlements at the very top of the wall. As men are now, even one in the bloom of youth could hardly lift it with both hands, but Ajax raised it high and flung it down. It smashed Epicles’ four-crested helmet and crushed the bones of his head to pieces, and he fell from the high wall like a diver, with no life left in him. Then Teucer wounded Glaucus, the brave son of Hippolochus, as he was coming on to attack the wall. Teucer saw his shoulder bare and aimed an arrow at it, and this made Glaucus stop fighting. He sprang down out of sight, for fear some of the Achaeans might see that he was wounded and taunt him. Sarpedon was stung with grief when he saw Glaucus leave him, but he did not stop fighting. He aimed his spear at Alcmaon son of Thestor and hit him. He drew the spear back again, and Alcmaon came down headlong after it, his bronzed armor clattering around him. Then Sarpedon seized the battlement in his strong hands and tugged at it until it all gave way together, and a breach was made through which many could pass.

Ajax and Teucer both turned on him. Teucer’s arrow struck the strap that carried the shield over his body, but Zeus saved his son from destruction, for he was not to fall by the ships’ sterns. At the same moment Ajax sprang at him and pierced the shield, though the spear did not go clean through it. It shoved Sarpedon back, so that he could advance no further. He gave up a little space by the battlement, though not all his ground, since he still thought to cover himself with glory. Then he turned and shouted to the brave Lycians, “Lycians, why do you fail me like this? For all my prowess, I cannot break through the wall alone and open a way to the ships. Follow close behind me. The more of us there are, the better.”

The Lycians, shamed by his rebuke, pressed closer around their counselor and king. The Argives, for their part, got their men into fighting order inside the wall, and a deadly struggle began between them. The Lycians could not break through the wall and force their way to the ships, and the Danaans could not drive the Lycians from the wall now that they had reached it. As two men, measuring-rods in hand, quarrel over the boundaries of a field they own in common and argue stubbornly for their rights though it is only a narrow strip, so now the battlements became a bone of contention, and the two sides beat one another’s round shields for possession of them. Many a man’s body was wounded by the pitiless bronze when he turned and bared his back to the foe, and many were struck clean through their shields. The wall and battlements were everywhere drenched with the blood of Trojans and Achaeans alike. Even so, the Trojans could not rout the Achaeans, who held on. As some honest hard-working woman weighs wool in her balance and checks that the scales are true, because she wants to win a pitiful wage for her little ones, so evenly was the fight balanced between them, until the time came when Zeus gave the greater glory to Hector son of Priam, who was first to spring toward the wall of the Achaeans. When he had done so, he cried aloud to the Trojans, “Up, Trojans, break the wall of the Argives and fling fire upon their ships.”

So he drove them on, and they rushed at the wall in one body, as he had ordered, and climbed the battlements with sharp spears in their hands. Just outside the gates lay a stone, thick at one end and pointed at the other, and Hector took hold of it. Two of the best men in a town, as men are now, could hardly have heaved it from the ground onto a wagon, but Hector lifted it easily by himself, since the son of scheming Cronus made it light for him. A shepherd picks up a ram’s fleece in one hand and finds it no burden. That is how easily Hector lifted the great stone and drove it at the doors that closed the gates, so strong and so firmly set. The doors were double and high, held shut by two crossbars that had only one key. He came close, then strode forward so that his blow would gain force, and struck the middle of them, leaning his whole weight against them. Both hinges broke, and the stone dropped inside, so heavy it was. The portals re-echoed with the sound, the bars gave way, and the doors burst open, one flying each way, from the force of the blow. Then brave Hector leaped inside, his face as dark as flying night. The gleaming bronze flashed fiercely about his body, and he had two spears in his hand. No one but a god could have withstood him as he flung himself into the gateway, and his eyes glared like fire. Turning to the Trojans, he called on them to scale the wall, and they obeyed. Some climbed straight over the wall while others came through the gates. The Danaans fled in panic toward their ships, and all was uproar and confusion.
